reason: General technique from this episode: a test that scans source or declarations to enforce a rule can pass while blind. Proving it catches a deliberate violation is the cheap check. Class-level, so later guard tests reuse it. Project level because its worked example names this repo's walk.

The same "prove it can fail before trusting green" discipline applies to a behavioural regression test for a fix, and that case currently has no trigger here; the procedure was only in metaform-development.
Behavioural regression proof for a UI fix was done correctly here (copy, revert, fail with the defect's value, pass with fix, delete scratch); recording that as the rule for the class.

A regression check was proven to fail on the reverted copy, but its assertion still passed for the wrong reason (it matched a later seat reply, not the held one). The proof step needs to require the assertion to name the exact output the fix must keep.

The elevenlabs regression check first passed with 1 request instead of 2 because its urlopen stub answered, and the answer was cached. Switching the stub to refuse exposed the second request. The copy-first procedure proved the fix.
The episode traced which path delivered an answer by editing the shared tree with probes and restoring by cp, which the existing shared-tree rule forbids; the probe-in-copy procedure is the lesson.

On 2026-10-14 the F4 agent's regression test passed on the shared tree only because a parallel agent had already landed the F3 fix there. Proof came from a /tmp copy built from HEAD's files plus a one-line hook, which failed on the defect's own assertion. The skill describes the copy but not this case.

A new CLI verb that syncs over the network failed the open-world evidence registry until it had a reasoned entry. The fix was the registry entry, and the walk stayed as it was. That is a repeatable pitfall for any module verb.

Ticket 574e48c5 (#16): a first mutant failed with AttributeError ('Project' object has no attribute 'id') before reaching the assertion, so it proved nothing until corrected. The 'nothing in home A' check looked at home/projects/proj/source_placement, a path the code no longer used, so it could never fail; a second mutant that writes into home A was needed to show it has teeth. The original _move_runs file was never committed, so a behaviour-reproducing mutant was the only proof available.

A race fix was judged by one green run; the trace showed narrow race windows only reproduce at a given worker count and in a fraction of runs, so the before/after proof needs repetition and enough concurrency.

The HEAD-copy "before" run first failed on a missing fixture file under the copy's tests/fixtures, not on the defect's assertion; copying the fixtures folder was needed before the real assertion failure appeared.
The guard-mutation skill lacks the seed trap: a new guarded field makes hand-seeded rows silently take the default branch, so a mutant check can look green for the wrong reason.

The episode wrote a Windows-only lock regression test and recorded that it "fails only on the Windows CI job without the fix; on Linux it passes before and after", without running it against the unfixed code. A platform-branch proof needs a forced branch, which the skill does not describe.
The before-run of a recall regression test failed on an incidental earlier assertion instead of the dock-count check that encodes the defect; reordering was needed before it proved anything.

The episode proved a regression test by an in-memory mutant through a scratch -p plugin, because a sibling agent was editing the same file; the skill only covers copy-aside. It also caught a green-looking -k run that selected 0 tests, which the skill does not warn about.

The before-run used a copy-aside and git-show-HEAD sequence with a trap that restored the shared tree on any exit. It was the clean way to show two new tests fail on HEAD and pass after, and the skill does not name it.

Two proof pitfalls hit this episode and absent from the skill: a mutant rewritten at the same byte size within one second reuses stale bytecode, so the test silently runs the old declaration; and a snapshot guard needs a column-add mutant that fails and a reorder that passes.

The mutation step copied server.py aside and restored it with cp while a sibling ticket was editing the same file. The skill names the race but not the restore method that avoids clobbering a sibling's writes; the episode shows the agent doing exactly the unsafe thing and only surviving by timing.

The skill told readers both to restore a shared-tree mutant by reversing one line (never cp back) and to restore with cp -p. Reconciled so the cp restore is allowed only where no sibling session can race it.

The browser-test proof was done ad hoc: the agent copied the test file over the HEAD page files and read the failing line to show the new follow assertion fails without the fix. The procedure should be in the skill, and the unfixed-copy check for an unrelated timing failure should be explicit.
A shared UI helper needs a mutant that fails on every item the probe lists, so a probe that finds nothing cannot pass for proof; this extends the mutation rule to browser probes.
The episode proved a runner end-to-end test by a mutant in a /tmp copy; the kill came from an eventually() timeout, a case the skill does not yet name, and the full bound makes the run slow to read.

After adding a dispatch verb, the MCP annotation guard failed on dispatch_wait and dispatch_spend, which the change did not touch. The episode recorded it as a defect in memory and left it, which is the right handling; the skill should say so for the next guard failure.
